This gap is addressed with a multi-stage framework, supported by a new benchmark of 19,998 IFRS regulation-disclosure pairs comprising 11,161 unanimous multi-LLM labels and 8,837 human annotations on items where the LLMs disagreed. The framework couples a three-stage domain-adapted sentence embedding pipeline (BERT masked language modeling on SEC EDGAR filings, unsupervised TSDAE and SimCSE adaptation, and supervised contrastive alignment) with a learned ensemble classifier that fuses frozen embeddings and LLM probability features from GPT-4.1, Claude Sonnet 4, and Gemini 2.5 Pro via Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) optimized gradient-boosted trees. On the disagreement set, the ensemble achieves 81.7% weighted F1, exceeding the strongest single LLM by 10.4 points and majority voting by 14.6 points, and outperforms eleven unsupervised aggregation baselines; the retrieval pipeline attains Recall@15 of 45.3% on unseen regulations. The dataset, model checkpoints, annotation platform, and classifier implementation will be publicly released.

title: SafeRoute-MAS: Coverage-Aware and Risk-Calibrated Message Routing for Multi-Agent Scientific Reasoning
abstract: We introduce SafeRoute-MAS, a coverage-aware, risk-calibrated procedure that keeps all specialist messages or removes one using only pre-integration information. On a sealed cache of 5,328 committees, its source-compatible operating point gains +1.80 percentage points (95% CI [+1.13, +2.52]) while removing 12.76% of message tokens. We also run 4,580 controlled integrations over a stratified 458-committee sample on a public gpt-oss-120b endpoint. The sample estimate is -0.09 points; design weighting to the original workload gives +0.94 points (95% CI [-1.31, +3.50]) and 18.72% acted-input reduction. A weighted token-matched comparison likewise does not establish a selector advantage (+1.68 points, CI [-1.27, +5.10]). Only 13 of 88 cached non-neutral labels (14.8%) retain direction by repeated-call majority. Expected-corruption UCL is 4.60% after weighting, but only 2 of 11 prespecified marginals pass the support/risk rule. We therefore propose a numerical qualification with Keep-All fallback, applied here retrospectively rather than validated prospectively.

title: Multi-Objective Scheduling of LLM-Based Multi-Agent Workflows in Cloud Computing
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been increasingly composed into multi-agent workflows to accomplish complex and multi-step tasks. As the open-weight models continue to close the performance gap with the proprietary ones, model parameters are becoming a less significant source of competitive advantage in the artificial intelligence market. Yet how these models are efficiently scheduled onto distributed infrastructure such as the cloud, with respect to overall latency, monetary cost and resource utilization, remains largely unaddressed in the literature despite being an increasingly critical problem. Existing agentic workflow frameworks mostly focus on output quality and task success rates over popular benchmarks, rarely accounting for execution dynamics of LLM-based agents such as inference latency, computation power of heterogeneous resources, cloud-specific billing period and resource provisioning overheads. Therefore, this paper formulates multi-agent scheduling in cloud computing as a multi-objective optimization problem that jointly minimizes makespan and cost while maximizing resource utilization. Building on this formulation, we propose MO-SAIC (Multi-Objective Scheduling of Multi-Agent Workflows in Cloud Computing), a scheduling framework comprising four multi-objective schedulers with Non-Dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II), Weighted-Sum Genetic Algorithm (W-GA), a multi-objective adaptation of Heterogeneous Earliest Finish Time (MO-HEFT) and a random baseline (RAND). We evaluate the schedulers from the workflow scheduling, multi-objective optimization and system perspectives to measure their overall performance, quality of their Pareto-optimal fronts and impacts of workflow topology, cloud resource composition and scalability parameters. We report the experimental results with their statistical significance via the Wilcoxon test.

title: Validating AI-Discovered Cloud Threats on Live Infrastructure: A Multi-Model, Multi-Cloud Study
abstract: Cloud infrastructure threat modeling lacks empirical validation of AI-discovered threats. We present a three-phase methodology of multi-agent threat discovery, automated exploit synthesis, and non-destructive live validation, and apply it to three commercial foundation models on two cloud architectures, validating each threat natively on the cloud (AWS, GCP, or Azure) it was discovered against. Of 233 AI-discovered threats, 103 were confirmed and 34 refuted (75.2\% precision, 95\% CI [67.3, 81.7]); 44 were conditional (the named mechanism refuted but an equivalent impact shown through another path) and 52 indeterminate. Multi-model discovery helped through breadth, not agreement: the three models together found 2.2$\times$ the confirmed threats of the best single model at comparable precision, while threats reported by several models were confirmed no more often than single-model ones. False positives were not architecture-specific: they asserted access or system state the deployment did not have. Threats coded in advance as observable configuration resolved cleanly more often than multi-step behavioral threats (72.5\% vs.\ 51.6\%), which were more often conditional, suggesting that models more often misidentify the exploitation mechanism than the underlying weakness. AI-assisted discovery is a practical input to security workflows when paired with empirical validation.

title: TriAgent: Granularity-Stratified Multi-Agent Routing with a Multilingual Semantic Cache and a Free Trust Signal for LLM Inference Pipelines
abstract: LLM-based information pipelines—retrieval, classification, entity linking, intent inference—share a structural cost problem: the reasoner LLM dominates the per-query bill, yet a large fraction of queries are trivially handled by far cheaper specialists. We present TriAgent, a generic multi-agent inference router that stratifies agents by contextual granularity (word / sentence / cross-sentence) and gates routing with a three-way Semantic Divergence Index (SDI). On two financial testbeds we report four findings. (i) The critic plateau is calibration-conditional: on FPB (where FinBERT is well calibrated, ECE=0.016) critic protocols collapse 1.5B-7B Qwen to a single F1≈0.87 (bootstrap CIs overlap), while a same-size 3-persona vote drops to 0.66; on TFNS (where the specialist collapses to F1=0.66) the critic plateau fails, falling below the LLM-alone baseline. (ii) A Shared Consensus Dictionary on multilingual sentence-BERT answers 95% of Chinese queries from an English cache at F1=0.99 — a cross-lingual canonicaliser at zero marginal cost. (iii) The same SDI doubles as a post-hoc LLM-hallucination detector at AUC=0.90. (iv) At a 10M-user scale the architecture saves 363M/year against a GPT-4 baseline. The router, cache, and trust signal are domain-agnostic and apply directly to LLM-based IR pipelines.

title: HyperMind: Claim Resolution and Reputation Tracking for Trustworthy Multi-Agent LLM Aggregation
abstract: The quality of knowledge produced by multi-agent generative AI systems depends not on the capability of individual agents but on the reliability of the communication layer between them. When agents disagree, that reliability is entirely invisible: no outcome is recorded, no agent is accountable, and the system learns nothing. This paper presents HyperMind, a protocol that makes disagreements productive by treating each resolved dispute as a verifiable calibration event, through three co-designed components: a seven-state Claim Resolution Finite State Machine (FSM) issuing signed provenance receipts; a Beta reputation system updated exclusively from FSM-verified outcomes; and DiversityGuard, which detects and interrupts premature consensus. On a 100-question enterprise benchmark spanning five domains, HyperMind achieves the lowest Brier score on all four tested LLMs; paired-difference 95% BCa confidence intervals exclude zero on two models (Gemma-4-26B [+ 0.0321,+ 0.0913], Wilcoxon p=0.0005, surviving Bonferroni correction across four models; Qwen-3.6-35B [+ 0.0021,+ 0.0737], p=0.037, not correction-surviving), though the n=100 evaluation is underpowered for the remaining two models (5-6% power). The full run costs \0.005 per 100 questions, and every resolved claim produces an auditable chain of custody over agent reliability.

title: When Is Debateability a Model Property? Cross-Interlocutor Validation in Multi-Agent Debate
abstract: Multi-agent debate (MAD) evaluations often treat resistance to false persuasion and receptiveness to truthful correction as model-level capabilities. We test whether such persuasion-derived scores support stable target-model inference in a controlled one-turn target–interlocutor persuasion setting. Across multiple models, interlocutors, and reasoning benchmarks, single-context scores fail to identify reliable target rankings and are strongly conditioned on the interlocutor. Leave-one-interlocutor-out evaluation shows that aggregating multiple interlocutors partially recovers a transferable combined signal, but the component behaviors generalize differently, with false-attack resistance remaining weakly transferable. Independently sampled response instability predicts acceptance of both false attacks and truthful corrections, indicating that answer revision is not inherently evidence of successful deliberation. In our downstream pruning setting, fixed-interlocutor rankings do not provide consistent cross-task evidence of agent contribution. These findings establish that interlocutor sampling is part of the measurement design and that single-interlocutor persuasion scores should not be interpreted as stable target-only properties of persuasion behavior without cross-interlocutor validation.

title: Rethinking Requirement-to-Code Traceability Through Single-Agent and Multi-Agent Approaches
abstract: Requirements-to-code traceability supports essential software engineering activities, including change impact analysis, maintenance, and regulatory compliance. Existing approaches typically rely on a retrieval-and-classification pipeline, which suffers from an inherent retrieval bottleneck: relevant source files that are not retrieved cannot be recovered during subsequent analysis. In this paper, we revisit requirements-to-code traceability in light of the substantially larger context windows offered by modern large language models, which make repository-scale analysis feasible without a separate retrieval step. We propose three approaches: a single-agent approach that analyzes the entire code repository in one pass, and two multi-agent approaches based on self-verification and multi-agent debate. Our evaluation shows that the single-agent approach substantially improves recall, achieving 80.9%, a gain of 38.6 percentage points (pp) over the state-of-the-art retrieval-based baseline, albeit with a 25.8 pp reduction in precision. By leveraging collaborative reasoning, the multi-agent debate-based approach achieves the best overall precision-recall balance, with 24.5% precision and 71.0% recall, yielding an F2 score of 49.5%. This represents an improvement of 7.5 pp over the state of the art and 2.7 pp over the single-agent approach. While the quantitative evaluation establishes the overall effectiveness of the approaches, the aggregate metrics alone explain little due to the considerable variability across results. Importantly, qualitative analysis provides key insights into highly variable quantitative results: the retrieval approach suits requirements that echo the code's vocabulary; single-agent, full-context reasoning suits well-documented, consistently named code; and multi-agent debate suits indirect, conflicting, or distributed evidence.

title: Test-Time Compute Scales Better with Parallel Agent Teams
abstract: Test-time scaling improves the performance of a fixed model by spending more computation at inference. There are two common ways to spend it on agents when a verifier can score every attempt. Best-of-N sampling runs many independent agents and keeps the best result but saturates quickly. One large team of collaborating agents can score higher but stops improving as it grows. Can we get the best of both? Our method, parallel agent teams, does so by sampling many small teams in parallel and keeping the best team's result. We test it on 12 long-horizon tasks from GPU kernels and formal proofs to exploit development. With a 27B model and a budget of 100 agents, parallel teams of ten beat parallel agents on 10 of 12 tasks and beat one team of 100 on all four tasks where we ran such large teams. At equal dollar cost the same parallel teams beat a frontier model on half the tasks. A simple statistical model shows that individual agents lose because their many samples have a low mean and that one large team loses because a single sample gets no gain from variance. Sampling many small teams in parallel balances a high mean with the gain from variance. Parallel agent teams thus offer a more effective way to scale test-time compute.

title: Failure Profiling and Reachable Trajectory Selection for Reasoning Distillation
abstract: Training smaller language models on reasoning solutions generated by a larger teacher model is the prevailing approach for transferring mathematical reasoning capabilities. However, the student tends to overfit the output distribution of the teacher and generalizes poorly when its own behavior at inference time deviates from the training data. Recent methods attempt to bridge this gap by incorporating error data, yet the corrective trajectories still reflect the reasoning patterns of the teacher, which the student cannot reliably reproduce, leaving the distribution mismatch largely unresolved. We propose a method, Failure Profiling and Reachable Trajectory Selection (FPRT), built on the insight that effective training data should be jointly determined by what the student fails on and what it can realistically learn. Our method first profiles the failure behavior of the student on each problem through repeated sampling, characterizing it in terms of error rate and error consistency to reveal qualitatively distinct failure modes. Each mode demands a fundamentally different training signal. The diagnosed mode then guides candidate generation from the teacher via distinct prompting strategies tailored to each failure type. Among the correct candidates, our method selects the one whose initial reasoning steps after the point of divergence are most reproducible by the student. These first corrective steps constitute the primary bottleneck, while the remaining steps follow an already corrected context and can therefore be continued more readily. This contrasts with standard reranking approaches, which score the trajectory as a whole and thereby dilute the signal at the critical reasoning transition. Experiments demonstrate that our method achieves the SOTA performance across the five benchmarks on both student backbones.

title: ReSUM: Reasoning-Driven Multi-Agent Framework for Query-Focused Summarization
abstract: LLMs excel at language tasks, but long-meeting QFS remains difficult due to complex speaker dynamics, sparse key information, and limited data. Meetings involve disfluencies, long transcripts and complex discourse. QFS have high risk of information omission, hallucination, even for advanced models such as GPT-4-mini and Gemini. Existing end-to-end methods compress retrieval, evidence extraction, and summary generation into a single pass, failing to handle the complex reasoning required for targeted meeting summaries. We propose ReSUM, a modular multi-LLM framework coordinated by a planner that orchestrates retrieval and summarization agents. By distilling teacher reasoning into query- and plan-conditioned retrievers and summarizers, ReSUM enhances long-context robustness, minimizes irrelevant exploration, and generates more faithful and comprehensive query-focused summaries. Experiments show consistent gains on query-focused meeting summarization benchmarks.

title: Plug-and-Play Verifier for Decoupling Process Reward in Stabilizing Long-Horizon Agentic Reasoning
abstract: Stabilizing long-horizon reasoning requires intelligent agents to sustain useful progress across successive reasoning steps and tool interactions. Such agents are typically trained with reinforcement learning (RL), where actor-critic RL uses a learnable critic network to estimate step advantages, while critic-free methods such as GRPO eliminate critic models and rely mostly on the group variants of sparse outcome-only rewards. Both reward types leave partially useful failed trajectories either implicit or indistinguishable from entirely unproductive ones, and as reasoning horizons grow, it becomes difficult to maintain consistent reasoning trajectories. In this work, we propose a \textit{plug-and-play verifier} framework for stabilizing long-horizon reasoning through explicit verification of intermediate reasoning artifacts. Specifically, the framework decouples process verification through a unified interface that extracts intermediate reasoning artifacts from agent running trajectories, evaluates them using domain-specific verifiers, and aggregates the verification scores as bounded process reward. Then, we combine our dense verified process rewards and the sparse outcome rewards through a two-stage post-training schedule. We showed that with plug-and-play verifiers, we further stabilize the reasoning steps as last-mile self-reflection and self-consistency. Typical evaluation on HotpotQA using Qwen3.5-4B achieves a superior accuracy (60.18\%), outperforming the standard GRPO baseline (57.73\%). Our results suggest that plug-and-play verifiers provide a modular approach to learn more stable and reliable reasoning behaviors over long horizons.

title: SMART: State-based Multi Agent Reasoning Traces for Verification-oriented Problem-Solving
abstract: Complex problems with limited context, such as claims, require a means to obtain additional knowledge necessary for solution reasoning. We propose a multi-agent framework, SMART, to obtain knowledge through capturing the implicit state of participating entities in a problem context. SMART curates the state knowledge as diverse, complementary and solution-salient premises using a variety of LLMs and a structured role-based prompt strategy. Using knowledge from these real-world verified curated premises, SMART's knowledge guided solution reasoning improves validation performance up to 20% on complex scientific claims spanning 3 datasets. We show that grounding premises in real-world knowledge is necessary and improves performance up to 5%.

title: Learning Multi-Agent Orchestration:Higher-Order Interactions in Policy Improvement
abstract: Learned orchestration has emerged as a promising paradigm for large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems, in which a central orchestrator selects agents and controls the information they receive throughout a task. Despite rapid empirical progress, existing methods train the orchestrator by crediting each decision with its own advantage, implicitly assuming that the other decisions in the episode stay fixed. This assumption fails in orchestration, where the contribution of each decision to the final outcome depends on the decisions preceding it, so the gain of a joint update is not the sum of its per-decision effects. To address this challenge, we introduce \textbf{IAPO}, an interaction-aware policy optimization framework that explicitly accounts for interactions among decisions. Specifically, IAPO exactly decomposes the performance difference between two policies into the effects of individual decisions and their interactions, which we prove can account for half of the attainable gain, and then optimizes both from sampled trajectories while certifying that every update is an improvement. On long-input versions of GSM8K, MATH, DROP, MBPP and HumanEval, against fifteen published multi-agent and workflow-search systems on the same 7B executor, IAPO's deployed plans reach the strongest system's accuracy with fewer tokens, and removing the interaction term costs 7 to 17 points of accuracy on code.

title: Aspect-wise Pairwise Tournaments for Test-Time Selection
abstract: Scaling test-time compute has proven highly effective at improving LLM reasoning. A popular method is best-of-n sampling, where a model generates many candidate solutions and one is selected. This motivates the question: how can we select the best candidate? When humans make choices, we find it more natural to compare two options than judge each in isolation. Additionally, when the options become complex, we like to judge the options one aspect at a time, such as comparing two job candidates on experience, communication, etc. In the test-time setting, candidate solutions should be judged in the same way. Here we introduce Aspect-wise Pairwise Tournaments (APT), which verifies by comparison and compares by aspect. Each matchup of a single elimination tournament is decided by a vote over multiple off-the-shelf aspect verifiers, each expressing a pairwise preference along its own aspect. Across five domains and three generator LLMs, APT improves over binary multi-aspect approval, self-consistency and reward model verification, with the largest gains on open-ended tasks. We find that both components matter; neither binary approval over the same aspects nor a generic pairwise judge at a matched budget matches APT. Because aspects are specified in natural language, APT also lets users steer selection toward properties they care about, better aligning with user preferences without needing to regenerate solutions. No component is trained, so APT transfers to new domains by simply rewriting prompts.

title: Debate to Deceive: Poisoning LLM's Fact-Checking via Game-Theoretic Multi-Agent Debate
abstract: Knowledge attacks on Large Language Models, such as manipulating fact-checking judgments, pose significant risks to AI reliability. Existing approaches -- adversarial suffix/template injection and single-agent self-reflection -- lack robustness across diverse defenses and are prone to confirmation bias and costly trial-and-error, respectively. We propose Debate-to-Deceive (D2D), a multi-agent debate framework grounded in human debate structure and rhetorical style, enabling agents to generate adversarial passages that are semantically coherent, rhetorically effective, and resistant to early confirmation bias. D2D formalizes the adversarial process as an evolutionary game in which agents adaptively evolve their rhetorical strategies (Logos, Pathos, Ethos) through competition. To manage the intractably large LLM output space, we decouple agent behavior into a strategic layer, which selects a rhetorical action from a compact strategy space via evolutionary-inspired learning dynamics, and a generation layer, where the LLM produces a concrete passage conditioned on that strategy and the debate context. On four fact-checking benchmarks (FEVER, HealthVer, CLIMATE-FEVER, and SciFact), D2D substantially outperforms existing attacks and evades most defenses.

title: Correlation limits the reliability of ensemble decision making with large language models
abstract: Multi-agent systems increasingly combine the votes of several Large Language Models (LLMs), assuming that an ensemble is more reliable than its members. The classical warrant, the Condorcet Jury Theorem, requires independent voters, yet models that share pre-training data, architectures, alignment, or prompts tend to fail on the same questions. This paper argues that the correlation between agents’ errors, which design choices influence but do not fix, is the decisive and most overlooked quantity in LLM ensemble decision-making. Within a model of exchangeable binary votes, we adapt known results on correlated juries. The effective number of independent voters, a variance-based effective sample size, is capped by the reciprocal of the correlation: a hundred agents correlated at 0.3 have the variance of about three independent ones. Majority accuracy plateaus below certainty and can fall below that of one agent. Adding samples from one model at a fixed temperature cannot raise that plateau, whereas different base models can; whether persona prompts can is empirical. We extend the effective-size result to unequal correlations and competences, give a moment estimator of the correlation with bootstrap intervals, and apply it to real models on MMLU: temperature samples and personas of one model are correlated at 0.85, five models from different developers at 0.38. We argue that semantic aggregation does not automatically escape correlated inputs, and propose a six-item reporting checklist for deployed ensembles. Among language models, consensus is not by itself evidence of correctness; among correlated agents, it may reflect redundancy.

title: Beyond Risk Cues: A Mechanism-Level Benchmark and Verifiable Debate for Scam Video Detection on the Web
abstract: Online scam videos pose significant threats to individuals and society. Existing studies primarily focus on binary classification, offering limited insights into how scams work and the reasoning behind detection decisions. Moreover, they often overlook the challenge of distinguishing scam videos from superficially similar non-scam content, such as advertisements, and the robustness of detection models against misleading arguments. These limitations hinder reliable scam video detection. To address these limitations, we introduce MechScam, a benchmark comprising 6,614 videos covering diverse scam mechanisms and non-scam categories. MechScam provides explanations supported by video evidence, annotations of potential scam elements and their context, and misleading arguments constructed from genuine evidence. Recognizing that genuine evidence can still be used to justify misleading conclusions, we further propose ScamCourt, a debate framework in which trained prosecution and defense debaters present opposing arguments, while a trained judge makes decisions based on a transcript with verified citations. Extensive experiments show that state-of-the-art MLLMs struggle to distinguish scam videos from similar non-scam content. ScamCourt outperforms larger MLLMs and same-backbone fine-tuned baselines, reducing false positives and showing stronger resistance to misleading arguments. Together, MechScam and ScamCourt contribute to more reliable and interpretable scam video detection. The dataset and code are available at https://github.com/SuperYFan/MechScam.

title: TRIO: Task Refinement with Individual Optimization for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
abstract: This paper studies retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which leverages external knowledge to improve the performance of language models. Despite the remarkable progress, current RAG approaches are still far from satisfactory due to inadequate retrieval and potential hallucinations. Towards this end, we propose a novel approach named Task Refinement with Individual Optimization (TRIO) for RAG. The core idea of our TRIO is to equip three well-designed agents with an iterative refinement paradigm by aligning their individual optimization objectives. Specifically, we first expand ambiguous queries with a query extension agent and quantify the reward based on the improved answer quality, which can be utilized to refine our agent for higher expansion efficiency. To enhance the retrieval quality, we include a unanimity voting to annotate the expanded query as insufficient or sufficient, and their generative outcomes are utilized as ground truth to optimize the judge agent. To further improve evidence utilization and answer accuracy, an answer agent is optimized with dynamic matching-based rewards with curriculum learning for final outputs. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmark datasets validate the effectiveness of the proposed TRIO in comparison with state-of-the-art approaches. Our code is available at https://github.com/yingtaoren/TRIO.

title: Beyond Division of Labor: How Roles Shape Feedback and Recovery in Multi-Agent Systems
abstract: Roles in multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems allocate decisions as well as work. In a Planner--Executor--Reviewer team, the Reviewer's approval can determine when the team submits an answer and receives corrective feedback. We study both functions by varying role instructions while holding agents, topology, call budget, and ground-truth evaluator constant, using three open-weight models on Omni-MATH and two on SciBench. Removing roles largely eliminates functional specialization without lowering first-pass accuracy. After a failed first answer, however, submission decisions matter: a role-structured Reviewer often withholds approval, so its team submits less often and receives fewer evaluator verdicts. In an exploratory comparison with feedback available to both teams, the role-free team recovers more often across all five model--benchmark settings. Two further analyses support the importance of feedback opportunities. In a post hoc comparison at equal numbers of verdicts, the pooled recovery difference is small (role-structured minus role-free: $+0.009$, 95% interval $[-0.014,+0.033]$). In an exploratory intervention on $400$ Omni-MATH problems with gemma-4, keeping the role prompts but forcing submission in every cycle raises recovery from $0.198$ to $0.613$; the paired comparison detects no difference from the role-free team. The takeaway is to evaluate roles through recovery after failure as well as specialization. For systems with reliable external feedback, this requires measuring who may submit, how often the team receives feedback, and which agents can act on it.

title: Genuineknowledge-KEOL at LLMs4OL 2026 Tasks Flagship, Reuse, and Taxonomy: Hybrid Training-Free Pipelines for Ontology and Taxonomy Discovery
abstract: Ontology learning traditionally requires substantial domain expertise and curated corpora. This paper presents our systems for the three tracks of the LLMs4OL 2026 shared tasks: Task A: end-to-end ontology learning from raw text; Task B: extension of a partial ontology with new concepts and relations extracted from text; and Task C: cross-domain taxonomy learning. Our approach is entirely training-free: no model is fine-tuned, and no external knowledge bases are introduced. Rather than a single shared pipeline, the three systems follow a common design philosophy—stage-wise construction that pairs the semantic reasoning of instruction-tuned large language models, deterministic post-processing, and task-specific modules—but each task instantiates this philosophy differently. For Task A, we instantiate this framework as a domain-aware, multi-stage pipeline that retrieves in-domain demonstrations to progressively extracts and refines ontology elements. For Task B, we extend partial ontologies through domain-aware candidate verification, while using a three-model debate and ensemble mechanism to resolve conflicting concept and relation predictions. For Task C, which requires substantial domain knowledge and involves datasets of varying sizes, we employ models with stronger domain expertise together with size-adaptive chunking and rule-guided taxonomy extraction. Our work showcases how carefully orchestrated prompting, retrieval, and deterministic rules can deliver strong ontology learning results in a fully training-free setting.

title: Peer Memory Changes Who LLM Agents Consult Without a Detected Gain in Answer Accuracy
abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems often reuse the same agents across tasks, creating an opportunity to draw on past interactions when deciding whom to consult. We study this form of memory with PeerMem, which saves MACE's LinUCB state and reuses it when the same agents return. Using six agents, a fixed set of 80 HotpotQA questions, and 12 paired lineages per model, we compare cold, warm, and shuffled initialization in an answer-exchange protocol with reference-answer feedback. Under stable evidence access, warm memory lowers pooled hindsight regret and increases consultation of other evidence holders on Qwen3-32B and Gemma-4-31B-it, while final token F1 differences remain uncertain. Qwen interaction traces further show that warm agents more often encounter peer answers that score above their own prior answers. We extend the evaluation to Qwen3.5-9B using freshly learned memory to compare warm and cold initialization under reassigned and paired stable roles. The primary changed-minus-stable final-F1 interaction is -1.38 points, with a 95% interval of [-3.50,+0.73]. Together, these experiments trace the effects of peer memory through consultation, answer revision, and final task performance.

title: Selecting LLM-Generated Hypotheses Raises Truth Beyond What an LLM Panel Expects: A Pre-registered Study on NAS-Bench-201 and HPOBench
abstract: LLM research-ideation systems aim for hypotheses that are both true and non-obvious, yet neither property can normally be checked. We build a testbed in which both can. Generators propose conditional interaction claims about two fully tabulated benchmarks, NAS-Bench-201 and HPOBench; every claim is verified exactly against the tables, and its non-obviousness is scored against a calibrated blind prior elicited from other LLMs. Excess truth measures how much more often a run's claims hold than this panel expects. Across a series of pre-registered stages with Claude and GPT generators, our main positive result is a simple two-stage step found by a harness optimizer: draft a large pool of claims, then select a subset in a separate call. For Sonnet on NAS-Bench-201, this step raised excess truth in every pre-registered test, including against a same-pool ablation that keeps only likely-true claims, without lowering precision. The gain comes both from credit for true claims and from avoiding near-miss false ones. In post hoc checks it held under every calibration, panel and truth rule we tried, and it exceeded random and type-filter selection from the same pools. Because kept claims recur across runs, the evidence weakens when runs and claims are resampled jointly, and it is not significant against Sonnet's own prior. Two secondary findings are also pre-registered. GPT makes real use of the results of cheap probes, beating shuffled and withheld controls, though not more efficiently than asking for more claims. Optimizing the harness for an LLM judge raised judge scores while sharply cutting precision for every generator.

title: From Delegation to Coordination: Learning Efficient Multi-Agent Deep Research
abstract: Multi-agent deep-research systems use delegation to parallelize search and keep long tool traces out of the main agent's context. Yet delegation helps only when task allocation and subtask execution are coordinated: the main agent must issue useful subtasks, while subagents must return reliable evidence. Existing training either optimizes only the main agent or broadcasts the same team advantage to all agents, which can reward misleading subagent reports and penalize useful ones. We introduce LEAD-RL (Learning Effective Agent Delegation with Reinforcement Learning), a joint main-agent-subagent training framework with contribution-aware credit assignment. A training-time rubric evaluates the research utility of each subagent report and gates its inherited team advantage, while final-answer correctness remains the only team reward; no token, step, or speedup reward is used. Across five benchmarks and two model families, LEAD-RL improves answer quality. On BrowseComp, it improves accuracy by 2.49 percentage points and reduces critical-path cost by 24.5% over joint training with shared team credit. During validation, accuracy increases by 6.78 points at approximately constant critical-path cost. These results show that contribution-aware credit assignment improves the quality-efficiency trade-off of multi-agent deep research.

title: HALight: Heterogeneous Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Traffic Signal Control under Lane-Level Missing Observations
abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning has shown great promise for traffic signal control. However, most existing methods rely on two key assumptions: (i) agents are assumed to be homogeneous with unified observation/action spaces; (ii) full and reliable lane-level traffic observations are available to all agents. In practice, urban road networks exhibit substantial structural heterogeneity (e.g., lane configurations and phase designs), while sensor failures and incomplete detector coverage often result in missing incoming lane measurements. Such issues can severely impair coordination and destabilize learning. To address these challenges, we propose HALight, a communication-enhanced heterogeneous multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for traffic signal control under lane-level missing observations. HALight supports intersection-specific observation and action modeling to accommodate heterogeneous intersections, and incorporates a lightweight one-hop neighborhood communication module to enrich spatial context when lane-level observations are partially unavailable. Moreover, HALight adopts a sequential policy update scheme to improve coordination among heterogeneous agents. Experimental results on two real-world road networks demonstrate that HALight outperforms representative homogeneous and heterogeneous baselines in terms of traffic efficiency and convergence behavior. The code and datasets used in this work are available at https://github.com/Huchenkaii/HALight.

title: JudgeMix: Judge-Guided Mixed-Rollout Data Synthesis for LLM Agents
abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on expert trajectories is a standard paradigm for training LLM agents. However, it suffers from a well-known training-inference distribution mismatch, calling for target-aware data synthesis strategies that ground the training data in the target model's native state distribution. To bridge this gap, emerging approaches incorporate the expert either to guide mixed rollouts alongside the target model, or to provide dense step-wise supervision. Nonetheless, existing methods apply expert assistance blind to the target model's inherent behavior: they either disrupt the rollout using sub-optimal random intervention heuristics, or they enforce indiscriminate uniform supervision that unnecessarily overwrites the model's already-correct actions. We introduce JudgeMix, a judge-guided data synthesis framework that dynamically interleaves the target model and expert based on step-wise semantic evaluations. JudgeMix queries expert guidance precisely when the target model struggles, ensuring high trajectory success rates while keeping the state distribution aligned with the target model. It additionally uses the judge evaluation to reweight expert supervision on different steps, preserving model's inherent valid behavior while correcting its errors. On two agentic tool-use benchmarks, AppWorld and AutomationBench, JudgeMix demonstrates consistent superior performance to existing methods, with improvements up to 10 pass@1 points.

title: DecArena: Evaluating Large-Scale Decentralized Multi-Agent Collaboration
abstract: Emerging personal AI agents raise fundamental scalability and privacy concerns for centralized multi-agent systems (MASs), which rely on a global orchestrator with broad access to agents, resources, and communication. In decentralized environments, global visibility is unavailable. Agents need to proactively discover non-local resources (e.g. tools, skills), and collaborate with other agents to solve tasks. We study decentralized multi-agent collaboration under graph-constrained communication, a natural reflection of human structures. Each agent observes only its local state and can interact only with neighboring agents. We introduce a benchmark with synthetic scalable distributed tool calling with 100K+ tools. Our experiments reveal that recent LLM agents struggle to discover non-local relevant resources and collaborate in decentralized setting. Moreover, standard reinforcement learning fails to reliably overcome this limitation, suggesting that decentralized MAS needs more explicit harness mechanisms for effective collaboration, even using SOTA LLMs. We then present a strong baseline \textbf{GraphHarness}, combining topology-aware warmup with self-improving LLM-based routing. Results show that GraphHarness substantially improves task success (+48.5) and produces higher quality collaboration (+30.6), while using fewer costs (+34.0) than baselines.

title: GuardianAgentFlow: Multi-Agent Coordination for Web Privacy Protection
abstract: Web agents need to use private context without unnecessarily disclosing it. Effective protection must distinguish between requests that may be sent after sanitization and those that must be withheld, while preserving the information needed for authorized tasks. We present GuardianAgentFlow, a multi-agent framework that mediates outgoing Web requests through an explicit release contract. A dedicated restriction check grounds permission in the user's instruction; a shared protection scope aligns rewriting with disclosure checking; and candidate-grounded feedback guides revision before transmission. Experiments on Web requests with human-reviewed intent labels show improved request-contract success, while controlled comparisons and role ablations identify the contributions of restriction handling, policy evidence, and candidate checking. Evaluations of action proposals from PrivacyLens and AgentDAM demonstrate complementary protection when mediation is composed with privacy-aware agents. Experiments with smaller mediation models show that the coordination benefit persists with reduced model capacity. Dedicated-server measurements show lower mediation latency than full-policy reasoning, while real-site browser tests quantify integration overhead.

title: CoLFA: Collaboration-Guided Lightweight Failure Attribution for LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
abstract: Failure attribution in multi-agent systems requires tracing error formation to identify the decisive error step and the responsible agent. However, agents' division of work and information exchange lead to Interleaved Steps and Cluttered Content, requiring models to link executions and check details in lengthy records. This makes it difficult to balance localization accuracy and token cost. We find that multi-agent collaboration also leaves records of how executions connect and content passes between them as results are formed, providing evidence for tracing error formation. Based on this observation, we propose CoLFA (Collaboration-Guided Lightweight Failure Attribution), which uses collaboration cues to organize the attribution input according to how results are formed, determining which steps are examined and how their content is presented. Through Handoff-Guided Step Expansion and Cross-Referenced Content Organization, CoLFA helps the model focus on examining error formation and the role of each decision while reducing the processing of irrelevant and repeated records. Across five settings spanning Who&When and LongRCA and three backbone models, CoLFA achieves the highest exact step-localization accuracy with the lowest token consumption. Compared with individual baselines in each setting, CoLFA improves accuracy by up to 37.50% and reduces token consumption by up to 97.6%.

title: Understanding the Effects of Multi-Agent Deliberation for Human-AI Decision-Making
abstract: Multi-agent deliberation (MAD), where multiple LLMs engage in structured discussion, improves AI performance on many benchmarks, but whether it helps humans make better decisions remains untested. We conduct two user studies on LLM-response-verification and fact-checking. We first compare MAD against common AI decision-support methods that isolate its two defining dimensions --- multiple AIs and multi-round interaction. We find MAD outperformed single-round AI assistance on both tasks; multi-round interaction was the main driver of this benefit, while a second AI added value when the single AI had room to improve. Then, we study two design choices in MAD --- AI persona and human engagement level --- finding a devil's advocate persona to lower accuracy and user experience, while humans' active participation in MAD improved accuracy in one task at the cost of frustration. We conclude by discussing implications for when, why, and how multi-agent deliberation can support human decision-making.

title: MLIRBench - A Benchmark and Dataset for Compiler and Hardware-Aware Reasoning
abstract: In recent years, large language models (LLMs) have become increasingly popular in software engineering and have performed well on different programming tasks. However, it is still difficult to know whether these models truly understand program behavior or whether they mainly rely on patterns learned from their training data. This distinction is particularly important for intermediate representations (IRs), where operations, dataflow, and execution semantics are explicitly represented. In this paper, we introduce MLIRBench, a benchmark for evaluating how LLMs reason about MLIR programs. MLIRBench uses a multi-agent pipeline to generate program mutations, validate their behavior through execution, and construct reasoning tasks from torch and linalg program pairs. The dataset contains 1,768 validated pairs, including 888 linalg pairs and 880 torch pairs, labeled as EQUIV, DIVERGE, or ERROR. We evaluated nine models, including five open-weight and four proprietary models. Gemini 3.1 Pro achieved the highest hard-label accuracy of 92.65% across all 1,768 pairs, counting unsuccessful predictions as incorrect. Across its 1,768 scored predictions, it achieved an aggregate score of 74.18 and a judge-assigned result-behavior score of 5.04/10. These results show that strong semantic classification does not necessarily imply accurate prediction of detailed execution behavior, highlighting a gap in current LLM reasoning over compiler IRs. By exposing this gap through execution-validated program pairs, MLIRBench provides a reproducible foundation for studying semantic reasoning over compiler IRs and related tasks such as program repair and semantic classification.

title: Open Challenges and Opportunities in Human-Agent Systems
abstract: Agentic AI systems increasingly undertake extended tasks and act on people's behalf, making human-agent interaction central to their effectiveness. Successful interaction requires understanding human perspectives, coordinating complementary capabilities, and maintaining productive relationships within socio-technical environments. This paper examines how foundations developed by the Autonomous Agents and Multi-Agent Systems (AAMAS) community inform these demands. We consider interactions ranging from individual human-agent partnerships to teams and larger groups, where participants differ in their roles, decision authority, capabilities, and objectives. We organize computational approaches around the connected challenges of understanding others and deciding how to interact with them. Theory of Mind, belief-desire-intention architectures, goal and plan recognition, inverse planning, and recursive reasoning provide mechanisms for representing and inferring partially observable mental states. Observer-aware planning, model reconciliation, and decision-theoretic communication connect these inferences to action, explanation, and information exchange. Together with shared autonomy, argumentation, and cooperative inverse reinforcement learning, these approaches offer foundations for agentic systems that account for evolving human knowledge, intentions, and expectations. We argue that progress requires treating human interaction as an ongoing decision problem shaped by uncertainty, interdependence, and potentially conflicting objectives.

title: MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation
abstract: Classical Sanskrit poses three challenges unresolved by single-call monolithic models: morphophonemic fusion Sandhi, dense nominal compounding Samāsa, and discourse-level zero-anaphora forced by poetic meter. We present MITRA-Swarm, a multi-agent architecture injecting explicit linguistic structure into an otherwise monolithic pipeline: a Sandhi-splitting agent, a parallel array of generalist gemma-4-26B-A4B-it and domain-specialized gemma-2-mitra-it translators, and a discourse-aware Ellipsis Restorer that consults corpus-derived register tags to avoid inventing active-voice subjects in impersonal legal and philosophical registers. Two separated judges evaluate quality: a routing judge ($J_{\text{route}}$, same model family as the generators) driving an internal critique loop, and an independent reporting judge ($J_{\text{report}}=$gpt-4o-mini, no shared vendor lineage) scoring every output exactly once. On a stratified benchmark of 1,000 verses across five registers (23,990 scored verdicts, 12-condition pre-registered ablation), the full swarm reaches $85.90$ MQM against a monolithic baseline of $85.27$ ($Δ=+0.63$, $p_{\text{adj}}=0.0018$, 95% CI $[+0.30,+0.97]$), and isolated discourse restoration alone accounts for $+0.44$ MQM ($p_{\text{adj}}=0.0288$), outperforming a call-count-matched self-refinement baseline by $+0.51$ MQM ($p_{\text{adj}}=0.0288$). Severe per-verse failures (MQM$<80$) fall from $9.0\%$ to $7.6\%$, at roughly $9\times$ the per-verse inference cost of the baseline. Additionally, $J_{\text{route}}$ scores its own family's outputs $2$-$7$ MQM higher than $J_{\text{report}}$ on every one of the 12 conditions, empirically motivating the two-judge split; and a preflight screen of a 192,151-entry retrieval index against all 12 evaluation works verifies 0 reference leaks across 269 runtime checks. These are small gains on a metric saturating near 85-86.
